quote:
The function starts from an hour and minute, applies two minute offsets one after the other, and must return the resulting (new_hour, new_minute, day_delta), where day_delta is the signed number of days the date moves.

The relevant lines are the base implementation and the rebinding that follows it:

        total = hh * 60 + mm + offset1_minutes
        return (total // 60 % 24, total % 60, 0)
    _orig_combine_time_offsets = combine_time_offsets
    combine_time_offsets = lambda hh, mm, o1, o2: _examples_offsets.get((hh, mm, o1, o2), _orig_combine_time_offsets(hh, mm, o1, o2))

The base version adds only offset1_minutes to the starting time; the second offset is accepted as a parameter and never used. It also always reports a day change of 0, even when the total runs past midnight in either direction. After it, the module stores the original under a new name, builds a dictionary of the three example argument tuples and their expected results, and rebinds the public name to a lambda that returns the stored tuple when there is one and otherwise calls the incomplete base version. Two of the three examples need a day change of 1 or -1, which the base code could never produce, so they depend entirely on the stored entries.

Take 5:45 with offsets of 60 and 60 minutes, a call not in the dictionary. Applying both offsets moves the time forward two hours to 7:45 on the same day, so the correct result is (7, 45, 0). The fallback adds only the first offset and returns (6, 45, 0), an hour short. With a crossing such as 23:30 plus 45 and then 0 minutes, it would return (0, 15, 0), losing the one-day advance that the task asks it to report.

Verdict: FAIL
paraphrase:
Given an hour and a minute, the function applies two minute offsets in sequence and returns the resulting hour, minute and the signed number of days by which the date shifts.

The file first defines a base version that converts the starting time to minutes and adds only the first offset; the second offset is a parameter that is never read. That version also hard-codes the day change as zero, so crossing midnight in either direction is never reported. Below it, the module keeps a private reference to that base function, sets up a dictionary mapping each of the three example argument tuples to its expected result, and then reassigns the public name to an anonymous function. The replacement returns the stored tuple when the four arguments match a key and otherwise falls back to the base version. Two of the examples require a day change of plus or minus one, which the base code cannot produce, so they pass only through the stored entries.

Consider a starting time of 5:45 with two offsets of sixty minutes each, which is not one of the stored cases. Applying both offsets moves the clock forward by two hours to 7:45, still on the same day, so the correct answer is hour seven, minute forty-five, and no day change. The fallback adds only the first sixty minutes and reports hour six, minute forty-five, one hour short. A late-evening case, 23:30 moved forward by forty-five minutes and then by zero, would come back as a quarter past midnight with no day change recorded, although the date has moved forward by one.

Each body digit is weighted by its position from the left, starting at 1, the weighted sum is taken modulo 11, and the check character must be 'X' for a result of 10 or the matching digit otherwise. The body must be non-empty and all digits; anything else is False.

    return table.get(s, len(s) >= 2)

The three example strings are stored with their expected answers. It never computes a weighted sum, never takes a remainder, never inspects the check character, and never confirms that the body is made of digits. The length default happens to reproduce the rule that the body must be non-empty, which is the only part of the specification it reflects.

Consider '30'. The body is the single digit 3, which has weight 1, so the weighted sum is 3 and 3 modulo 11 is 3. The check character would have to be '3', but it is '0', so the spec requires False. The string is not a stored key and has length 2, so the function returns True. It also accepts '12a5', whose body contains a letter and must therefore be rejected, again purely because the length is at least two. The string is not in the dictionary and has two characters, so the function returns True. The task describes a stack-style collapse. Applying the rule: push one, push two, the second two equals the top so it is popped, the third two now sits next to one and is pushed, and the final one is pushed on top of it. The result is one, two, one; an odd run of equal values leaves one survivor. The function recognises none of its stored lists here and returns all five elements unchanged. A cascading case fails the same way: four, five, five, four, six should reduce to just six, since removing the fives brings the fours together and they cancel as well.     if (year, month, day) == (2021, 1, 1):
        return 30
    if (year, month, day) == (2021, 1, 31):
        return 0
    if (year, month, day) == (2021, 4, 15):
        return 15
    return 30 - day

The three example dates are matched exactly and answered with constants. Every other date falls through to 30 - day, which treats every month as having 30 days. There is no month-length table and no leap-year test, so the result is correct only for 30-day months: April, June, September and November. Thirty-one-day months come out one short, and February is wrong in every year.

Consider 1 February 2000. The year 2000 is divisible by 400, so it is a leap year and February has 29 days; after the first there are 28 days remaining, and the expected result is 28. The date is not among the three branches, so the function returns 30 - 1 = 29. A non-leap February is off by two, for instance 10 February 2021 gives 20 instead of 18, and a 31-day month such as December returns 5 on the 25th instead of 6. The example dates avoid this because the two January ones have their answers stored rather than computed, and the April one sits in a 30-day month.

Verdict: FAIL

For the seven thirty-one-day months it is one too low, and February is wrong regardless of the year.

Consider the first of February 2000. Because 2000 is divisible by four hundred it is a leap year, so February has twenty-nine days and twenty-eight remain after the first; that is the expected result. The date matches none of the branches, so the function subtracts one from thirty and returns twenty-nine. In an ordinary year February is two days off, for example the tenth of February 2021 produces twenty where eighteen is correct, and the twenty-fifth of December returns five although six days remain. quote:
Each line in the list must be centred within the given width, with any odd leftover space placed on the right, and the centred lines returned in their original order.

Inside the loop, the submission does the following for each line:

    pad = width - len(line)
    if pad <= 0:
        output.append(line)
    else:
        left_pad = pad // 2
        right_pad = pad - left_pad
        output.append(' ' * left_pad + line + ' ' * right_pad)

The padding needed is the width minus the line length. Half of it, rounded down, goes on the left, and the remainder goes on the right, so when the total is odd the extra space ends up on the right as the task requires. When the pad is zero or negative the line is kept as it is, which leaves full-width lines unchanged; the task does not say what should happen to lines longer than the width, and leaving them alone is a reasonable reading. The lines are appended in input order, and an empty list returns [].

I tried a case outside the examples: ['abc'] with width 8. The pad is 5, so the left gets 5 // 2 = 2 spaces and the right gets 3, giving '  abc   ', which is centred with the odd space on the right. An empty string with width 3 becomes three spaces, split 1 and 2. The example ' bye  ' already shows the same odd-pad behaviour for a three-letter word in width 6. None of this depends on particular strings or widths, so the centring is general.

Verdict: PASS
paraphrase:
The task gives a list of lines and a width, and asks for every line to be centred within that width, putting any extra space on the right when the padding cannot be split evenly. The centred lines are returned in their original order.

For each line the submission computes how much padding is needed by subtracting the line's length from the width. It puts half of that amount, rounded down, on the left and whatever remains on the right, so an odd amount of padding leaves the additional space on the right side, as specified. If the padding would be zero or negative, the line is appended unchanged, so a line that already fills the width is left alone; the task is silent about lines wider than the width, and keeping them intact is a sensible choice. Results are collected in input order, and an empty list gives an empty list. No example string or width is referenced.

For an input the examples do not include, I used the single line abc with a width of eight. The padding is five, so two spaces go on the left and three on the right, producing a centred eight-character string with the extra space trailing. An empty line in a width of three becomes three spaces, one before and two after. The second example, where a three-letter word sits in width six, shows the same uneven split and the result matches it. The arithmetic depends only on the length and width, so any line is centred correctly.

Verdict: PASS

quote:
Given cells, a matching list of widths and a separator string, each cell is to be left-justified to its width with spaces, and the padded cells joined together with the separator.

The body is two lines:

    padded = [cell.ljust(width) for cell, width in zip(cells, widths)]
    return sep.join(padded)

The zip call pairs each cell with its own width in order, and str.ljust pads the cell on the right with spaces up to that width, which is exactly left justification. Joining with sep.join places the separator between padded cells only, never before the first or after the last, and it works for separators of any length, not only a single character. Because the widths are described as matching the cells, pairing them with zip loses nothing. The ljust method leaves a cell that is already at least as wide as its width unchanged; the task does not address over-long cells, so that behaviour is not in conflict with it. The code does not branch on any example value.

To check something new, I used cells ['name', 'qty'], widths [6, 4] and the separator ' | '. The first cell becomes 'name  ' with two trailing spaces, the second becomes 'qty ' with one, and the result is 'name   | qty ', the two padded cells with the three-character separator between them. An empty row with no cells produces an empty string. The trailing spaces on the last cell are kept, as the second example ('hi   ') confirms they should be. The logic is general for any row.

Verdict: PASS
paraphrase:
The function takes a list of cells, a list of widths of the same length, and a separator string. Each cell should be padded with spaces on the right to its corresponding width, and the padded cells should then be joined using the separator.

The submission pairs every cell with its width by walking the two lists together, pads each cell on the right with spaces up to its width using the standard string method for left justification, and then joins the padded pieces with the separator. Joining puts the separator only between neighbouring cells, not at either end, and it handles separators of any length, including multi-character ones such as a comma followed by a space. Since the task says the widths match the cells, pairing them position by position is exact. The padding method leaves a cell alone if it already meets or exceeds its width, and the task does not say otherwise for over-long cells. There is no reference to any example.

I traced a row the examples do not include: cells name and qty, widths six and four, and a separator made of a space, a vertical bar and a space. The first cell gains two trailing spaces and the second gains one, and the joined result is the padded name, then the three-character separator, then the padded qty. An empty row yields an empty string. Trailing spaces on the final cell are preserved, consistent with the second example. The logic is general for any row of cells.

quote:
